review.headline: A strong opening ruined by 13.Na5, then a tough comeback through tactics at moves 18 to 23

sections.text: You started well. Your Italian setup with 4.d4 and 5.h3 gave you a space edge, and after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 the engine liked you at +1.5 once 7.d5 gained more space and kicked a knight around.

Then the middlegame slipped. 12.Nb3 was a mistake (+1.5 to +0.1); 12.a4 was better. Black replied 12...c5, but the engine's 12...Nxe4 was stronger. You then played 13.Na5??, which left a piece to be taken, and 13...Qxa5 swung the game to -3.5 for you.

You kept fighting, and your opponent gave it back. 17...f5?? was a blunder, and you answered with 18.Qxh5!. Then 21.Bh6! put a bishop en prise on purpose and 22...Qf7?? walked into 23.Qxf5!, which won material and put you at +4.4.
After that you simply converted. Trading queens with 26.Qxf7 Rxf7 left a winning endgame, and the d-pawn marched home: 39.d6 and 42.d8=Q ended the game. Your opponent resigned after 44 moves.

review.turning_point: 13.Na5 left a piece to be won; the recovery came when 17...f5 and 22...Qf7 gave you the chances back.
review.focus: At 13.Na5 you went for the knight jump without checking whether the knight could be taken. 13.a4 Nc7 kept the advantage; check each piece's safety before moving.

review.headline: A clean, patient win where you punished a loose knight move with a mating shot

sections.text: This was your best-played game of the batch at 93.6 accuracy. You met 2.Nc3 and 3.Nf3 with the solid 3...d6, 4...Be7 and 7...O-O. Against 5.Bg5 you played 5...h6 and recaptured calmly after 6.Bxf6 Bxf6, keeping the game equal.

You also handled the central tension well. 16...d5 was the right break at the right time. After 17.exd5 cxd5 18.cxd5 Nxd5 you were back to equal material with active pieces, and 19...Nb4 kept White's bishop and queen busy.

White went wrong with 20.Nh2?, which took the knight off f3 and opened the long diagonal toward g2. The engine wanted 20.Re3. You played 20...Qc6 at once, putting the queen and the bishop on b7 on that diagonal, and the evaluation moved to +1.4.
21.Rac1 ignored the threat, and 21...Qxg2# ended the game with mate on the diagonal you had prepared.

review.turning_point: 20.Nh2 removed the knight from f3 and left g2 exposed; 20...Qc6 aimed everything at it.
review.focus: Keep doing what you did here. Your 20...Qc6 shows the habit to keep: after the opponent's move, ask which defender just left. Nothing from this game needs fixing.

review.headline: A calm Petrov game thrown away by one tempting knight capture at 9...Nxf2

sections.text: This was a Three Knights Petrov and you played it sensibly. You met 4.d4 with 4...exd4, developed with 5...Nc6, 6...Be7 and 7...O-O, and the engine had it around -0.4, a normal small edge for White.

White's 8.O-O-O put the king on the queenside and 8...Ng4 was a fine active move. After 9.Bxe7, though, you had to take back. The engine wanted 9...Qxe7, simply winning the bishop back with a level game.

Instead 9...Nxf2 went for a fork (d1, d3, f2, h1), hitting the queen on d3 and the rooks. But it ignored the bishop sitting on e7 attacking your queen. 10.Bxd8 took your queen first, and after the trades on d3 and d8 you were left down a lot of material.
The evaluation went from -0.7 to -5.2 in one move and White just had to finish: 12.Nd5 and 13.h3 were enough. You resigned in a lost position.

review.turning_point: 9...Nxf2 went after a fork but allowed 10.Bxd8, losing your queen.
review.focus: At 9...Nxf2 you looked for a fork before checking what was attacking you. Always ask what your opponent's last capture threatens first; 9...Qxe7 was calm and good.

review.headline: A short game where your knight walked into trouble and a missed capture at 6.Ng3 decided it

sections.text: You opened with 1.d4 and 2.Nc3 and followed with 3.d5, gaining space against 2...Nc6. Black's knight went to a5 at move 3 and the engine already liked your side at +1.8 there.

The first slip was 4.Bd2, which let some of that advantage go. The engine suggested 4.b4 to chase the knight, with the idea 4...Nc4 5.e4 Nb6 6.e5 Ng8. After 4...e6 you then played 5.Ne4, and that move opened the d2 bishop's line onto the knight on a5, a discovered attack. It looks good, but 5.e4 was the safe move and 5.Ne4 dropped you to -2.7.

Black answered 5...Nc4, which was a blunder in turn and brought the position back to level. You then needed 6.Nxf6+ Qxf6 7.Bc3, but 6.Ng3 retreated and let the knight run free. 6...Nxb2 picked up a pawn and the knight on b2 stayed annoying for the rest of the game.
The last two moves, 8.Bc3 and 9.e3, left more material hanging. 8.dxe6 was the engine move, and 9.e3 left a piece to be won. You finished four points down in material.

review.turning_point: 6.Ng3 gave up the chance for 6.Nxf6+, which would have kept the position balanced.
review.focus: At 6.Ng3 you retreated when a capture was available. Before you retreat, list every capture and check for both sides; 6.Nxf6+ was there.

review.headline: A level Bishop's Opening where a free piece went untouched at 11...g5 and the attack followed

sections.text: This was a normal Bishop's Opening and you handled it well. The engine had it dead level for the first ten moves. You developed with 3...Nf6 and 4...d6, got your king safe, and after 9...Nd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 you had traded into a comfortable position.

Then your opponent gave you a gift. 11.Kb1 swung the evaluation to +1.8 for you, because the bishop on c4 was left without protection. The engine wanted 11...Bxc4, and after 12.Bxf6 Bxa2+ 13.Kxa2 Qxf6 you would have been clearly better. Instead 11...g5 pushed a pawn in front of your own king and gave the whole advantage back (-0.9).

From there White's h-pawn did the work. 13.h4 and 14.hxg5 opened lines against you, and 14...Nxg5 was a mistake; 14...Qxg5 was the better recapture. After 15.Bh4 pinned the knight on g5 against your queen, you still had 15...Bxc4 available, but 15...f6 let it all fall apart (-5.1).
The rest was a technical finish for White: 16.Bxe6+, 17.Qxh6, then 18.Nd5 and 19.Nxf6+ tore open your king. You resigned after 24.Qh6+.

review.turning_point: 11...g5 passed up 11...Bxc4, which would have punished 11.Kb1 and kept you clearly better.
review.focus: When your opponent blunders, as with 11.Kb1, look at every capture and check before you make a quiet pawn move. 11...Bxc4 was the move, and 11...g5 only weakened your own king.

sections.text: You played a sound Scotch with 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 and then 5.Bc4?!. After 5...Nxd4 6.Qxd4 Nc6 7.Qd5 Qf6 8.Bg5 Qg6 you had a normal position with the queen active in the middle.

sections.text: The trouble began with 9.h4?? and 10.h5??. The quiet 9.O-O Bb4 kept the position safe. After 10...Qxg5 you were down a bishop, with 11.Qxf7+ Kd8 only giving you some practical chances.
You fought back well with 12.O-O?! Qf6 13.Qd5 Ne7 14.Qd2 d6 15.Re1. Black then blundered with 15...Be6??, and you found the best reply, 16.e5!, to swing the game.
After 17.exd6 Bxc4?? you found 18.dxe7+!, and Black's king was driven to 18...Ke8, when 19.exf8=Q+ Kxf8 20.Qb4+ Kg8 21.Qxc4+ won back the bishop. You finished with 42.Rg8#.

review.turning_point: 15...Be6?? gave you the opening, and 16.e5! was the right move to use it. After that, 18.dxe7+! won back everything you had given up.
review.focus: At 9.h4 and 10.h5 you pushed a pawn into an unfinished attack. 9.O-O Bb4 kept your king safe, so castle before you start pawn storms.

review.headline: A Danish Gambit where you took everything offered, then 15...Qc5?? gave it back

sections.text: You accepted the Danish Gambit with 2...exd4 and 3...dxc3, then 4...cxb2, taking three pawns. 5.Bxb2 recaptured one, but you were up material (+2). 6...Be7? was a slight slip; 6...Bb4+ 7.Nc3 was stronger.

9...b6? gave White more play, and 10.Ng5 Bxg5 11.Qxh5 traded pieces. But after 12.Qh3? you found 12...d5!, with the bishop on c8 attacking the queen as a discovered attack. 13.Qg3?? then 13...dxc4! won a piece for you.

You were comfortably ahead. 14...Qe7?! was a slight inaccuracy, and then 15.Nd5 hit your queen. 15...Qc5?? left the bishop on g5 hanging, and the evaluation went from +0.3 to -4.6; 15...Qd8 was the way.
16.Qxg5 won the bishop back, and 17.Ne7+ Kh8 18.e6+ finished the job. Mate came at move 20, with 20.Qxf6#.

review.turning_point: 15...Qc5?? moved the queen but left the bishop on g5 undefended, and the sequence from 16.Qxg5 was winning for White.
review.focus: At 15...Qc5, see which of your pieces the queen was defending. 15...Qd8 kept g5 covered.

review.headline: A Caro-Kann that went wrong on 4.d5?? and kept getting worse

sections.text: In the Caro-Kann you gave up a pawn with 3.Nc3 dxe4. The right plan was 4.Nxe4, but 4.d5?? lost the thread (+0.3 to -1.5). 4...Nf6 5.Bc4 e6 followed.

6.Bg5?? pinned the knight on f6 against the queen on d8, but it ignored 6.dxe6. Black's 6...Bb4?? was a mistake, though (-3.7 to -0.6), and 6...cxd5 was the correct reply. Then 7.Bxf6?? gave up your bishop; 7.dxe6 was the move.
From there the game ran away. 8.dxc6?! allowed 8...Bxc3+, 9.Kf1 Bxb2 (-4), and 11.c7 Bxa1 left you down nine. 12.cxb8=Q was a consolation, but resigning was right.

review.turning_point: 4.d5?? gave up your central pawn structure and the opening edge; 6.Bg5?? and 7.Bxf6?? finished it.
review.focus: At move 4, take the pawn back with 4.Nxe4. In gambit-like positions, recapturing material first beats pushing the pawn.

review.headline: A good Italian that slipped away with 18.e5??

sections.text: Against 3...h6 you played the principled 4.d4, and after 4...Qf6 5.dxe5?! Nxe5 6.Bb3 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 d6 the game was fine. 8.Bd2 Bxc3 9.Bxc3 was solid, and 9...a6?? gave you a chance.
You found 10.Nxe5!, the best reply, and after 10...dxe5 11.Qd5 you came out clearly ahead. 12.Qxe5 Qxe5 13.Bxe5 and 14.Bxc7 won material (+2), so you were comfortably better at +4.
Then 17.Rac1? gave away some of it (the engine preferred 17.Rad1), and 18.e5?? was the real blunder (+2.5 to -0.8). 18...Ne2+ hit the king and the rook on c1, and 19...Nxc1 left you down material.
21.Bxb7?? made it worse, and 27.g3? sealed the endgame. 28 moves of good play from you, but the mistakes at moves 17 and 18 gave the game away.

review.turning_point: 18.e5?? dropped a +2.5 advantage in one move, because 18...Ne2+ attacked your king and rook.
review.focus: At 18.e5, before pushing a pawn, check whether the opponent's knight has a check that wins something. 18.Rc4 kept things together.

review.headline: A Scandinavian where you were doing well through the opening, but 14.Qb3 and 15.Rad1 lost it

sections.text: You met the Scandinavian with 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qd6 4.d4 Bf5, and 5.Nf3 was fine. After 5...Nc6 6.d5 Ne5? you were at +3.0, but 7.Be2?? let a good chunk of that go. 7.Nb5 was the right way to hit the queen.
8.O-O exd5 9.Re1?? was another miss, with 9.Nb5 stronger. Black took with 9...Nxf3+?, and your 10.Bxf3+! recaptured with check from the rook on e1. After 10...Be7 11.Nxd5 you were up to +4.
You kept the edge through 12.Bf4 Qc5 13.c3 c6, but 14.Qb3?? was the big mistake, dropping from +3.4 to +0.5. The line 14.Re5 cxd5 15.Rxf5 kept the advantage.
15.Rad1?? made it worse, because 15.Re5 Bd3 16.Bg4+ was better. Black missed 15...Qc4 and played 15...Be6??, but 16.Be3?? gave the edge back and you resigned after 16...Qc4.

review.turning_point: 14.Qb3?? let a clearly better position drop to equal, and 15.Rad1?? finished the job. 14.Re5 was the move that kept the pressure.
review.focus: When you are ahead, look at your opponent's threats before you add a quiet move. At 14.Qb3 and 15.Rad1 the rook on e1 stayed passive, and 14.Re5 or 15.Re5 would have kept your pieces active.
